questions.question: What is the main job of a package / dependency manager?
options: Install, update, remove, and track software or libraries (often including versions) in a consistent way
Replace version control entirely
Compile every language down to machine code
Host course assignments on Canvas
questions.explanation: Package managers automate installing and managing dependencies so machines and projects stay reproducible.

questions.question: Why do software projects use dependency managers instead of copying library source into every repo by hand?
options: Hand-copied libraries can never run
Dependency managers delete the need for testing
Managers make versions, updates, and shared libraries easier to declare and reproduce across machines
GitHub rejects repositories that contain any third-party code
questions.explanation: Declaring dependencies (and locking versions) is more maintainable than vendoring everything manually and hoping everyone has the same copies.

questions.question: Which statement best describes **layers** of package management?
options: One tool always manages the OS, Python, and Node.js the same way
Only npm can install operating-system packages on Linux
Poetry replaces Apt on Ubuntu
OS package managers (for example Homebrew or Apt) install system tools; language managers (for example Poetry or npm) manage libraries for a specific ecosystem
questions.explanation: Different layers of the stack use different managers. Matching the tool to the layer (OS vs language) is a core idea of the unit.

questions.question: Homebrew and Apt are primarily used to manage…
options: Only React component libraries
Operating-system / system-level packages and tools on a machine
Docker images exclusively
Git commit messages
questions.explanation: These are OS package managers: install things like `wget`, `curl`, or language runtimes onto the machine itself.

questions.question: In Apt, what is the difference between updating the package index and upgrading installed packages?
options: Refreshing the index downloads current package metadata; upgrading installs newer versions of packages you already have
There is no difference; the commands are synonyms
Upgrading only refreshes metadata; updating uninstalls everything
Updating is Mac-only; upgrading is Windows-only
questions.explanation: Think: refresh the catalog first, then upgrade the software already installed from that catalog.

questions.question: Poetry is primarily used for…
options: Managing only macOS GUI applications
Building Docker images from a Dockerfile
Managing Python project dependencies and environments
Editing HTML without a browser
questions.explanation: Poetry belongs to the language layer: it tracks Python dependencies for a project and runs code in that project’s environment.

questions.question: When you add a library with a language package manager (for example Poetry or npm), where does that dependency usually “belong”?
options: Only to the operating system, forever, for every project
Only inside the git `main` branch name
Only on Docker Hub
To the project: it is recorded in project metadata and installed into that project’s environment or package folder
questions.explanation: Project-level managers record deps in files like `pyproject.toml` or `package.json` and install them into an isolated project environment / `node_modules`, not as a vague global OS change.

questions.question: Why might a script import successfully with `poetry run python …` but fail with a plain system `python3 …` and `ModuleNotFoundError`?
options: Because `python3` cannot run `.py` files
Because the library was installed into Poetry’s project environment, which system Python does not automatically use
Because Poetry forbids all imports
Because Java must compile Python first
questions.explanation: Virtual environments isolate dependencies per project. System Python has its own site-packages and will not see Poetry-installed libraries unless you install them there too (usually a bad idea for coursework projects).

questions.question: What problem do **project environments** (Poetry’s env, Node’s local `node_modules`, etc.) help prevent?
options: Different projects needing different versions of the same library and stepping on each other
The need to ever use version control
CPU usage on laptops
Writing documentation
questions.explanation: Isolation means Project A can depend on library v1 while Project B uses v2, without forcing one global install to satisfy both.

questions.question: What is npm primarily for?
options: A Python-only virtual environment tool
Debian’s only OS package manager
The default package manager for Node.js / JavaScript projects
A replacement for Docker Compose
questions.explanation: npm manages packages and scripts for the Node ecosystem, analogous to how Poetry serves Python projects.

questions.question: What is the role of a file like `package.json` or `pyproject.toml`?
options: It stores your GitHub private SSH key
It is the compiled binary of your application
It replaces the need for a README
It declares project metadata and dependencies (and often scripts) so others can recreate the same setup
questions.explanation: These manifests are how a project says “here is what I depend on.” They are checked into version control so the setup is reproducible.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a **lock file** (for example `package-lock.json` or Poetry’s lock file)?
options: To encrypt your source code so classmates cannot read it
To pin exact resolved versions of dependencies (and sub-dependencies) so installs stay reproducible
To list only the operating system packages on the machine
To disable `git commit`
questions.explanation: Manifests often allow version ranges. Lock files freeze the exact graph that was resolved so “works on my machine” is less likely when someone else installs later.

questions.question: Before adding a new third-party dependency to a project, which consideration fits best with this unit?
options: Weigh benefit vs cost: maintenance, security, license, size, and whether you really need it
Always add it — more libraries are always better
Only add dependencies that have never been updated
Dependencies should never be locked to a version
questions.explanation: Dependencies are not free: they bring code you did not write, plus update and security risk (as readings like left-pad illustrate).

questions.question: Why can installing a language runtime from an OS package manager sometimes be a poor fit for modern app tooling?
options: OS packages are never allowed to include compilers
Language runtimes can only be installed with Docker
Distro packages can lag behind the versions your tools expect, so version managers (for example nvm) are often used instead
OS package managers cannot access the network
questions.explanation: Apt’s Node package, for example, is often older than what Vite/React tooling wants. Version managers install current runtimes without fighting the distro’s defaults.

questions.question: What is a dependency **graph** in this context?
options: A chart of git commits only
A UML class diagram required by Docker
The folder layout of your home directory
The tree of packages you depend on, including the packages *those* packages depend on
questions.explanation: You rarely depend on one library in isolation. Package managers resolve a whole graph of transitive dependencies — which is why lock files and careful upgrades matter.

questions.question: Which statement best compares OS package managers with language package managers?
options: They are interchangeable; use either for any language or OS task
OS managers install tools for the machine; language managers install libraries for a project/ecosystem — they solve related problems at different layers
Language managers can only install kernels; OS managers can only install React
You should never use both on the same computer
questions.explanation: You often use both: Apt/Homebrew for system tools and runtimes, Poetry/npm for project libraries. Knowing which layer you are changing avoids confusion.
